new_statements.quote: The stress on words is similar to that of Spanish; an apostrophe after a vowel shows that it is stressed. For words without an apostrophe (the vast majority), words ending in a vowel or the letter s are stressed on the next-to-last syllable. Words ending in a consonant other than s are stressed on the last syllable. The letters i and u are semivowels (pronounced like y in yes and w in win) when followed by any vowel, or when preceded by a, e, or o, so i and u don't count as separate syllables in this case, unless they're followed by an apostrophe, which shows that they are full, stressed vowels

new_statements.rule_in_words: Spanish-type default: stress falls on the penultimate syllable when the word ends in a vowel or in -s, and on the final syllable when it ends in any other consonant; a final closed syllable (other than -s) attracts stress. Words that deviate carry an apostrophe (or optionally an acute accent) after the stressed vowel, e.g. di'a, roma'nicas, podera', grama'tica, polisi'a, ida' (attested in the same source). Adjacent i/u form diphthongs (non-syllabic) unless apostrophe-marked. Elsewhere on the page the word cuo 'whose' is given the note 'Stress is on the u'.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked exceptions written with an apostrophe after the stressed vowel (optionally an acute accent instead); the suffix section adds that a final vowel is dropped before suffixation only if it is unstressed, so apostrophe-marked final vowels (e.g. -ida') are stressed finals. No other exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for the orthographic word; an a-priori design rule (constructed language), not an observation of speech. The reading 'weight-sensitive' is chosen because the rule is the Spanish pattern (closed final syllable other than -s takes stress, otherwise penult) plus lexical marking; a catalog that files Spanish under a different label should file Romanova the same way.
new_statements.identity_note: Romanova (glottocode roma1338, ISO rmv) is an a-posteriori pan-Romance auxiliary language first published online in 1999/2000 by David Crandall (with Robert Hubert and Michael Edwards per nl.wikipedia). The only descriptive source is the creator's own web grammar (AOL site c. 1999-2008, now romanova.altervista.org); the stress rule is a prescriptive design rule, not an observed one, and Glottolog lists no descriptive references. Do not confuse with Romanova, O. I., editor of the Jazyki mira volumes (unrelated surname hits in our check CSVs).

new_statements.quote: La maniero de montri la silabon kun emfazo similas la hispanan manieron: apostrofo post vokalo montras ke ĝi havas la emfazon. Se vorto ne havas apostrofon (kiel la plimulto), kaj la lasta litero de la vorto estas vokalo aŭ la litero s, la silabo antaŭ la lasta silabo havas la emfazon, kiel en Esperanto, sed se la lasta litero estas konsonanto krom s, la lasta silabo havas la emfazon. La litero i estas prononcataj kiel j, kaj la litero u kiel ŭ, kiam iu vokalo sekvas ilin, aŭ kiam a, e aŭ o estas antaŭ ili, do ili ne estas apartaj vokalaj sonoj ĉikaze, se ili ne estas sekvata de apostrofo, kiu montrus ke ili estas apartaj vokaloj
new_statements.translation: The way of showing the stressed syllable resembles the Spanish way: an apostrophe after a vowel shows that it carries the stress. If a word has no apostrophe (like the majority), and the last letter of the word is a vowel or the letter s, the syllable before the last syllable carries the stress, as in Esperanto, but if the last letter is a consonant other than s, the last syllable carries the stress. The letter i is pronounced as j [y], and the letter u as ŭ [w], when any vowel follows them, or when a, e or o precedes them, so in that case they are not separate vowel sounds, unless they are followed by an apostrophe, which would show that they are separate vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Spanish-type system: default penultimate stress in words ending in a vowel or -s, final stress in words ending in any other consonant; words that deviate carry a written apostrophe after the stressed vowel (optionally an acute accent, 'kiel en la hispana' = as in Spanish, the text layer); i and u next to another vowel are glides and do not count as syllables unless apostrophe-marked.
new_statements.exceptions: Apostrophe-marked words (e.g. preterite -o'/-io', the text layer); the same page (line 30) allows an acute accent above the vowel instead of the apostrophe.
new_statements.identity_note: Romanova is a constructed language (Crandall, with Hubert and Edwards); there are no dialects. The three works are the same text in three presentations (English original on AOL 2000, Esperanto version, IAL wiki mirror); the Esperanto version was read from the live romanova.altervista.org site rather than the listed 2003 Internet Archive copy, which was unreachable (web.archive.org refused connections on 80/443 by automated download).
